q: Who designed and built the first known mechanized printing press in Europe?
explain: Gutenberg, a German craftsman, originated a method of printing from movable type in Europe and used his press to print the Gutenberg Bible around 1455.
hook: Gutenberg = 'good' Bible, first press in Europe.

sources.title: Johannes Gutenberg | Britannica
sources.quote: Johannes Gutenberg is known for having designed and built the first known mechanized printing press in Europe. In 1455 he used it to print the Gutenberg Bible, which is one of the earliest books in the world to be printed from movable type.

sources.title: The Gutenberg Bible at the Library of Congress: A Resource Guide
sources.quote: A monument in the history of typography, the Gutenberg Bible was the first large-format typographic book printed in Europe. Crafted in Mainz, Germany in 1454/1455 by Johannes Gutenberg and his partner, Johannes Fust

q: In which German city did Gutenberg complete the Gutenberg Bible?
explain: Gutenberg completed the Bible about 1455 working at Mainz, Germany; he spent most of his working life in Strassburg and Mainz.

sources.title: Gutenberg Bible | Britannica
sources.quote: so called after its printer, Johannes Gutenberg, who completed it about 1455 working at Mainz, Germany.

sources.title: The Gutenberg Bible at the Library of Congress: A Resource Guide
sources.quote: Printed in Mainz, Germany in 1454/1455 by Johannes Gutenberg and Johannes Fust

q: The Gutenberg Bible is also known as the how-many-line Bible?
explain: The Latin text was printed in 42-line columns, which is why it is also called the 42-line Bible.
hook: 42 lines: the answer to everything, printed.

sources.title: Gutenberg Bible | Britannica
sources.quote: The three-volume work, in Latin text, was printed in 42-line columns

sources.title: The Gutenberg Bible at the Library of Congress: A Resource Guide
sources.quote: the Gutenberg Bible (also known as the 42-line Bible)

q: What device, conceived by James Watt in 1765, made the Newcomen-type steam engine far more efficient?
explain: While repairing a model Newcomen engine, Watt noticed its waste of steam; in May 1765 he came upon the separate condenser, which he patented in 1769.
hook: Watt fixed the waste: condense somewhere else.

sources.title: James Watt | Britannica
sources.quote: In May 1765, after wrestling with the problem of improving it, he suddenly came upon a solution—the separate condenser, his first and greatest invention.

sources.title: Newcomen steam engine | Britannica
sources.quote: While repairing a model Newcomen steam engine in 1764, Watt was impressed by its waste of steam. In May 1765, after wrestling with the problem of improving it, he suddenly came upon a solution—the separate condenser, his first and greatest invention.

q: In what year was the first recorded Newcomen atmospheric steam engine erected?
explain: Thomas Newcomen's first recorded engine was erected near Dudley Castle, Staffordshire, in 1712, and was used mainly to pump water out of mines.

sources.title: Thomas Newcomen | Britannica
sources.quote: The first recorded Newcomen engine was erected near Dudley Castle, Staffordshire, in 1712.

sources.title: Newcomen steam engine | Britannica
sources.quote: The advent of the Thomas Newcomen steam engine in 1712 created an important new market for iron

q: What message did Samuel Morse send on May 24, 1844, to open the Washington-Baltimore telegraph line?
explain: The Bible verse (Numbers 23:23) was suggested by Annie Ellsworth, daughter of the commissioner of patents.

sources.title: Today in History - May 24 | Library of Congress
sources.quote: On May 24, 1844, Samuel F. B. Morse dispatched the first telegraphic message over an experimental line from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore. The message, taken from the Bible, Numbers 23:23 and recorded on a paper tape, had been suggested to Morse by Annie Ellsworth, the young daughter of a friend.

sources.title: Telegraph | US House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives
sources.quote: May 24, 1844 | Surrounded by an audience of Congressmen, Samuel Morse sent the first official telegraph from the Supreme Court Chamber, then located in the Capitol, to his partner, Alfred Vail, in Baltimore. He tapped the message, "What hath God wrought!"

q: Morse's first government-funded telegraph line ran from Washington, D.C., to which city?
explain: Congress funded a demonstration line about 60 km (35 miles) long between Washington and Baltimore, opened to public use on May 24, 1844.

sources.title: Telegraph | Britannica
sources.quote: In 1843 Morse obtained financial support from the U.S. government to build a demonstration telegraph system 60 km (35 miles) long between Washington, D.C., and Baltimore, Md.

sources.title: Today in History - May 24 | Library of Congress
sources.quote: Samuel F. B. Morse dispatched the first telegraphic message over an experimental line from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore.

q: Which partner of Samuel Morse received the 1844 "What hath God wrought" message in Baltimore?
explain: Vail, a skilled mechanic, is credited with many contributions to the Morse system, including the make-and-break key.
hook: Vail at the other end of the wire.

sources.title: First telegraph message, 24 May 1844 | Library of Congress
sources.quote: sent by Morse on the wire from the Supreme Court chamber in the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., to his assistant, Alfred Vail (1807-1859), who was stationed at the Mount Clare railroad depot in Baltimore, Maryland.

sources.title: Telegraph | US House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives
sources.quote: Samuel Morse sent the first official telegraph from the Supreme Court Chamber, then located in the Capitol, to his partner, Alfred Vail, in Baltimore.

q: Who was awarded U.S. patent 174,465 for the telephone on March 7, 1876?
explain: The patent is often called the most valuable ever issued by the U.S. Patent Office because it described both the instrument and the concept of a telephone system.

sources.title: Telephone - Invention, Alexander Graham Bell | Britannica
sources.quote: On March 7, 1876, Bell was awarded U.S. patent 174,465. This patent is often referred to as the most valuable ever issued by the U.S. Patent Office, as it described not only the telephone instrument but also the concept of a telephone system.

sources.title: Who is credited with inventing the telephone? | Library of Congress
sources.quote: Bell was granted US Patent Number 174,465 for an "Improvement in Telegraphy" on March 7, 1876

q: What was the surname of the assistant Bell summoned in the first telephone speech transmission on March 10, 1876?
explain: Bell transcribed the words in his lab notes as "Mr. Watson—come here—I want to see you."

sources.title: Alexander Graham Bell | Britannica
sources.quote: He first produced intelligible speech on March 10, 1876, when he summoned his laboratory assistant, Thomas A. Watson, with words that Bell transcribed in his lab notes as "Mr. Watson—come here—I want to see you."

sources.title: Who is credited with inventing the telephone? | Library of Congress
sources.quote: it was March 10, 1876 that Bell declared to his assistant, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you!" over the lines of his working telephone, as he wrote in his laboratory journal.

q: Which rival inventor filed a caveat on a similar telephone method just hours after Bell filed his patent on February 14, 1876?
explain: Bell's application was allowed over Gray's caveat on the basis of its earlier filing; the priority question has been controversial from the start.

sources.title: Alexander Graham Bell | Britannica
sources.quote: Bell filed a patent describing his method of transmitting sounds on February 14, 1876, just hours before Gray filed a caveat (a statement of concept) on a similar method.

sources.title: Telephone - Invention, Alexander Graham Bell | Britannica
sources.quote: On the basis of its earlier filing time, Bell's patent application was allowed over Gray's caveat.

q: Who is generally credited with inventing the phonograph in 1877?
explain: Edison's first phonograph recorded sound as indentations in tinfoil wrapped around a rotating cylinder; he announced it on November 21, 1877.

sources.title: Phonograph | Britannica
sources.quote: the invention of the phonograph is generally credited to the American inventor Thomas Edison (1877). His first recordings were indentations embossed into a sheet of tinfoil by a vibrating stylus; the tinfoil was wrapped around a cylinder that was rotated as the sounds were being recorded.

sources.title: November 2017: Thomas Edison | U.S. Census Bureau
sources.quote: Edison announced the cylinder phonograph on November 21, 1877, and demonstrated the invention by playing "Mary Had a Little Lamb" on one of the invention's foil cylinders.

q: Which inventor coined the name "gramophone" for his disc-record sound system patented in 1887?
explain: Berliner's earliest gramophone patent was No. 372,786, awarded November 8, 1887.

sources.title: The Gramophone | Library of Congress
sources.quote: As a name for the whole operation the inventor coined the word "gramophone" (in early advertisements it was often written Gram-o-phone). His earliest patents were number 372,786, awarded November 8, 1887

sources.title: Phonograph | Britannica
sources.quote: These "records," as they came to be known, could be played on a reproducing machine Berliner named a Gramophone.

q: Berliner's gramophone recorded sound on what kind of medium, instead of Edison's cylinder?
explain: In 1887 Berliner traced sound grooves in a spiral on a flat disc rather than a helix on a cylinder, a design that lasted about 100 years in record players.

sources.title: Phonograph | Britannica
sources.quote: Improvements in Edison's process followed, notable among which were Emil Berliner's innovation in 1887 of tracing sound grooves in a spiral on a flat disc rather than in a helix on a cylinder.

sources.title: The Gramophone | Library of Congress
sources.quote: With the vibrations fixed into the zinc, the disc could be placed on a turntable and the sound reproduced with a steel stylus. This is how the earliest disc records were eventually made.

q: What material did Edison settle on for the filament of his practical 1879 incandescent light bulb?
explain: After testing many materials, Edison's lab first got a commercially promising lamp in October 1879 using carbonized cotton thread; he applied for the patent on November 4, 1879.

sources.title: November 2017: Thomas Edison | U.S. Census Bureau
sources.quote: He spent months examining materials, including metal wire, human hair, and even coconut husks, before settling upon a carbon filament.

sources.title: The Carbon-Filament Lamp | Thomas A. Edison Papers, Rutgers
sources.quote: In the early morning hours of October 22 1879, they began what Charles Batchelor called "some very interesting experiments on straight carbons made from cotton thread

q: In what year did the Wright brothers make the first powered, controlled airplane flight?
explain: The Wright Flyer first flew on December 17, 1903; the brothers made four flights that day.

sources.title: 1903 Wright Flyer | National Air and Space Museum
sources.quote: the Wrights' first powered airplane flew at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, making a 12-second flight, traveling 36 m (120 ft), with Orville piloting.

sources.title: 120 Years Ago: The First Powered Flight at Kitty Hawk - NASA
sources.quote: After several unsuccessful attempts, on Dec. 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright completed the first powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft known as the Wright Flyer.

q: Near which North Carolina town did the Wright brothers make their first powered flight?
explain: The flight took place at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk; the brothers had been testing gliders there since 1900.

sources.title: 120 Years Ago: The First Powered Flight at Kitty Hawk - NASA
sources.quote: on Dec. 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright completed the first powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft known as the Wright Flyer.

sources.title: The Wright Brothers Made History at Kitty Hawk | National Air and Space Museum
sources.quote: At 10:35 a.m., on December 17, 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright made history in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

q: Which Wright brother piloted the first successful powered flight on December 17, 1903?
explain: Wilbur won a coin toss and made an unsuccessful attempt on December 14; on December 17 it was Orville's turn, and his flight succeeded.
hook: Wilbur won the toss, Orville won the sky.

sources.title: 1903 Wright Flyer | National Air and Space Museum
sources.quote: Repairs were completed for a second attempt on December 17. It was now Orville's turn. At 10:35 a.m. the Flyer lifted off the beach at Kitty Hawk for a 12-second flight, traveling 36 m (120 ft).

sources.title: 120 Years Ago: The First Powered Flight at Kitty Hawk - NASA
sources.quote: Orville Wright completed the first powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft known as the Wright Flyer. The flight lasted just 12 seconds, traveled 120 feet

q: How many seconds did the Wright brothers' first powered flight last?
explain: The first flight covered 120 feet; the best flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds.

sources.title: 120 Years Ago: The First Powered Flight at Kitty Hawk - NASA
sources.quote: The flight lasted just 12 seconds, traveled 120 feet, and reached a top speed of 6.8 miles per hour.

sources.title: 1903 Wright Flyer | National Air and Space Museum
sources.quote: making a 12-second flight, traveling 36 m (120 ft), with Orville piloting. The best flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 255.6 m (852 ft) in 59 seconds.

q: Who noticed in 1928 that a mold growing in a bacterial culture stopped the bacteria's growth, leading to penicillin?
explain: Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Ernst Chain and Howard Florey for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect.

sources.title: Sir Alexander Fleming – Facts - NobelPrize.org
sources.quote: In 1928 he saw that in addition to bacteria, a mold fungus had begun to grow in a bowl and that the bacteria's growth had been impeded in the vicinity of the mold. He concluded that the mold contained a substance that was effective against bacteria. The substance was given the name penicillin

sources.title: Sir Howard Florey – Facts - NobelPrize.org
sources.quote: After Alexander Fleming's 1928 discovery that a certain mold produced a substance called penicillin that inhibited the growth of bacteria

q: According to the 1945 Nobel presentation speech, which mould species contaminated Fleming's culture?
explain: The mould belonged to the Penicillium group (brush moulds), which is why the substance was named penicillin.

sources.title: Physiology or Medicine 1945 - Presentation Speech - NobelPrize.org
sources.quote: It was soon realized that most of the species of Penicillium did not form it at all, and a closer scrutiny showed that the species which polluted Fleming's culture was Penicillium notatum.

q: At which research laboratory was the transistor invented in 1947?
explain: Bell Labs scientists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the invention.

sources.title: 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics | Nokia Bell Labs
sources.quote: Bell Labs scientists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their invention of the transistor

sources.title: Transistor - Innovation, Bell Labs | Britannica
sources.quote: Working closely together over the next month, Bardeen and Brattain invented the first successful semiconductor amplifier, called the point-contact transistor, on December 16, 1947.

q: In what year did John Bardeen and Walter Brattain produce the first point-contact transistor?
explain: Their semiconductor amplifier was further developed by William Shockley; all three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.title: William B. Shockley – Facts - NobelPrize.org
sources.quote: In 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain produced a semiconductor amplifier, which was further developed by William Shockley. The component was named a "transistor".

sources.title: Transistor - Innovation, Bell Labs | Britannica
sources.quote: Bardeen and Brattain invented the first successful semiconductor amplifier, called the point-contact transistor, on December 16, 1947.

q: What were the only letters received when UCLA sent the first ARPANET message to SRI on October 29, 1969?
explain: The team was trying to type "login," but the SRI system crashed after the "l" and "o"; Kleinrock later quipped it meant "lo and behold."
hook: Lo and behold: the internet's first word.

sources.title: The Day the Infant Internet Uttered its First Words | Leonard Kleinrock, UCLA
sources.quote: It took place at 22:30 hours on October 29, 1969. ... The transmission itself was simply to "login" to SRI from UCLA. They succeeded in transmitting the "l" and the "o" and then the system crashed! Hence, the first message on the Internet was "lo"

sources.title: Lo and behold: The internet | University of California
sources.quote: UCLA graduate student Charley Kline got as far as typing in the first two letters of the word "login" when the network crashed. Hence, "Lo."

q: Vinton Cerf co-developed the TCP/IP protocols with which DARPA program manager?
explain: Kahn asked Cerf, then at Stanford, to collaborate on new protocols for sending packets across the ARPANET, producing TCP and IP.

sources.title: TCP/IP | DARPA
sources.quote: DARPA's Robert Kahn (who joined the Information Processing Techniques Office as a program manager in 1972) asked Vinton Cerf of Stanford University to collaborate on a project to develop new communications protocols for sending packets of data across the ARPANET. That query resulted in the creation of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Internet Protocol (IP), most often seen together as TCP/IP.

sources.title: DARPA vignettes: ARPANET
sources.quote: He and Robert Kahn, then the director of DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) and who in 1976 hired Cerf as a program manager, began work on what would become the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Internet Protocol (IP).

q: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN?
explain: Berners-Lee wrote the first Web proposal in March 1989 and had the first Web server and browser running at CERN by the end of 1990.

sources.title: A short history of the Web | CERN
sources.quote: Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, invented the World Wide Web (WWW) in 1989, while working at CERN.

sources.title: Tim Berners-Lee | W3C
sources.quote: Sir Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while at CERN, the European Particle Physics Laboratory, in 1989. He wrote the first web client and server in 1990.

q: At which trade event did Apple introduce the iPhone on January 9, 2007?
explain: Apple's press release datelined Macworld San Francisco described the iPhone as a mobile phone, a widescreen iPod and an Internet communications device in one.

sources.title: Apple Reinvents the Phone with iPhone - Apple Newsroom
sources.quote: MACWORLD SAN FRANCISCO—January 9, 2007—Apple® today introduced iPhone, combining three products—a revolutionary mobile phone, a widescreen iPod® with touch controls, and a breakthrough Internet communications device
